lane.name: Big-tent Americana and stomp-clap folk
lane.definition: Old Crow Medicine Show, the Avett Brothers, Mumford & Sons, the Lumineers, Brandi Carlile: the festival-scale Americana mainstream.

albums.label: Nettwerk
albums.description: Produced by David Rawlings, the string band's national debut fuses old-time and bluegrass instrumentation with punk-scaled energy, most famously on 'Wagon Wheel' (built from a Bob Dylan chorus fragment by Ketch Secor). It is rowdier and more raucous than traditional old-time music, aimed at festival crowds rather than folk-revival purists. It is for hearing a record that helped launch the festival-scale Americana boom of the 2000s-2010s.
albums.lineage: Bridges old-time and bluegrass tradition (X4) with a punk-energy, festival-scaled string-band sound that seems to foreshadow the stomp-clap-folk wave of the Avett Brothers and Mumford & Sons.

albums.label: American Recordings
albums.description: Produced by Rick Rubin, the Avetts' major-label debut smoothed their earlier punk-folk roughness into fuller, string-and-piano-arranged Americana, the title track and 'January Wedding' built for big emotional payoffs and festival-crowd singalongs. It kept their brothers' close harmonies and confessional lyrics but scaled the sound to arenas. It is for hearing the moment stomp-clap folk pivoted from underground string-band roughness to mainstream festival Americana.
albums.lineage: Grows out of the Avetts' earlier punk-folk scrappiness and string-band roots, redirected toward a festival-scale Americana sound akin to what Mumford & Sons and the Lumineers would soon ride commercially.

albums.label: Island Records/Glassnote Records
albums.description: The London band's debut defined the stomp-clap-folk sound proper: banjo strum building to shouted group choruses, quiet-to-loud dynamics borrowed as much from indie rock as from folk revival, on hits like 'Little Lion Man' and 'The Cave.' It is unapologetically anthemic, built for festival main stages rather than folk clubs. It is for hearing a central template of the 2010s festival-folk boom.
albums.lineage: Sounds like the festival-Americana energy of Old Crow Medicine Show and the Avett Brothers turned into a UK indie-folk formula, a template for the stomp-clap-folk wave of the early 2010s.

albums.label: Sub Pop
albums.description: Originally self-released and sold at Seattle shows before Sub Pop picked it up, the band's debut leans on three-part harmonies, piano and violin melodies, and steady, festival-ready percussion on songs like 'Rivers and Roads.' It is warmer and more communal than Mumford & Sons' bombast, closer to campfire harmony singing scaled up. It is for hearing the softer, more indie-rock-adjacent wing of the stomp-clap-folk boom.
albums.lineage: A Pacific Northwest, Sub Pop variant of the festival-folk wave the Lumineers and Mumford & Sons rode, sounding closer to indie-pop harmony singing than to old-time string-band roots.

albums.label: Dualtone
albums.description: The band's self-titled debut, driven by the singalong stomp-clap of 'Ho Hey,' offers a leaner, more American-radio-friendly take on stomp-clap folk: acoustic guitar, cello, minimal percussion, and audience-participation hooks. It is for hearing stomp-clap folk at its most streamlined and commercially dominant.
albums.lineage: Sounds like a stripped-down American counterpart to Mumford & Sons' folk-revival formula; alongside the Avett Brothers, it helped define the festival-Americana mainstream of the 2010s.

albums.label: Stax
albums.description: After a career in quieter folk music, Rateliff reinvented himself with a horn section and Stax-style soul-revival energy on 'S.O.B.,' a stomp-and-shout single that became a festival-circuit anthem far bigger than his earlier solo folk records. It swaps banjo strum for horns and gang vocals but keeps the same communal, crowd-participation energy as the rest of this lane. It is for hearing the soul-revival cousin of stomp-clap folk's festival-anthem instinct.
albums.lineage: Shares the festival-crowd, singalong-anthem instinct of Mumford & Sons and the Lumineers but channels it through horn-driven soul that sounds indebted to Stax, an adjacent branch of big-tent Americana.

albums.album: By the Way, I Forgive You
albums.label: Low Country Sound/Elektra
albums.description: Carlile's sixth album fuses big-voiced folk-rock balladry with orchestral strings on 'The Joke' and 'Every Time I Hear That Song,' scaling festival-Americana emotion to arena size. It is more vocally virtuosic and personal than the genre's usual crowd-singalong mode. It is for hearing Americana's festival mainstream at its most emotionally direct.
albums.lineage: A singer-songwriter-driven, less banjo-dependent branch of the festival-Americana mainstream, sounding closer in vocal scale to 1970s folk-rock than to stomp-clap folk proper.
key_tracks: Every Time I Hear That Song

albums.label: Mulberry Records
albums.description: Swampy, familiar-sounding country rock that draws on Bobby Charles-style Southern groove without feeling derivative, closer to Americana's big-tent songcraft tradition than to Red Dirt's bar-band rowdiness. Telecaster twang and an easy drawl carry warm, unhurried story songs. It is for hearing where the festival-Americana mainstream and the Southern songwriter tradition overlap.
albums.lineage: Sits at the overlap of the big-tent Americana festival scene and the Southern/Texas songwriter tradition, closer to swampy roots-rock songcraft than to stomp-clap folk's banjo-strum anthems.

albums.label: Mercury Nashville/UMG Nashville
albums.description: The husband-and-wife duo of Michael and Tanya Trotter mix soul and gospel vocal power with Americana songwriting on this major-label debut, their trading, dueting vocals drawing on both Stax soul and festival-Americana's big-emotion instincts. Horns and close harmonies push the songs toward shouted, church-sized climaxes. It is for hearing gospel-soul vocal tradition meeting the big-tent Americana and country circuit.
albums.lineage: A gospel-and-soul-rooted branch of the festival-Americana mainstream that sounds akin to Brandi Carlile's emotional bigness; the duo later collaborated with Zach Bryan.
